baseline.sampleParagraph: Group projects is a good way for students working together and it can be really useful sometimes but there are also issues that come up like when people don't communicate well and this can affect the whole team's mark which happens quite often especially with big groups, see Robbins (2021) who talks about this a lot in his research on team dynamics generally.
baseline.pillar1_clarityPrecision: This sentence runs to 65 words with three separate ideas stapled together. 'Is a good way' and 'can be really useful sometimes' say almost nothing - vague filler where a specific claim belongs. Clarity means saying exactly what you mean: which issue, how often, with what effect.
baseline.pillar2_structure: There's no topic sentence - the reader can't tell what this paragraph is about until they've read the whole thing. No clear claim, evidence, judgement sequence. It reads as one long thought rather than a structured paragraph.
baseline.pillar3_engagementWithDiscourse: Robbins (2021) is mentioned but not used - 'talks about this a lot' reports that a source exists without saying what it found or why it matters. This is citation without engagement.
baseline.pillar4_presentation: The citation format itself needs checking against the required style - 'see Robbins (2021) who talks about...' isn't a standard in-text citation format. Small presentation details like this affect the overall impression, even when the content is sound.

decidedValue.note: All five context packs authored: baseline, criminology, sports-journalism, psychology, banking-and-finance.

baseline.essayExcerpt: Group work is frequently cited as a valuable component of higher education, offering students the opportunity to develop collaborative and interpersonal skills alongside subject knowledge (Osei and Bramwell, 2022). However, its effectiveness depends significantly on how responsibilities are distributed within the group.
baseline.whyEssayRegister: Third person, no personal pronouns. A claim supported by a citation. Formal vocabulary ('significantly', 'component'). The writer's own experience is absent - this argues a general point, not a personal one.
baseline.reflectiveExcerpt: When our group started the project, I assumed everyone would contribute equally. That wasn't quite what happened - two of us ended up doing most of the planning, and I'm still not sure why the others held back. Looking back, I think I should have set clearer roles from the start.
baseline.whyReflectiveRegister: First person throughout. Informal, conversational phrasing ('I'm still not sure why'). Follows the ERA structure in miniature: what happened (Experience), what it might mean (Reflect), what to do differently (the seed of Take action). No citation - the evidence is the writer's own experience, not a source.

wOpen.learningOutcomes: By the end of this course, you will be able to: write with clarity and precision, structure a paragraph so it argues rather than reports, integrate sources actively using the 'voices' technique, apply the four pillars as a self-review checklist, and adapt your register to the genre a task requires.
wOpen.overviewAndJustification: This course builds on the basics of getting a draft down. Here, the focus shifts to argument: how to make your writing not just correct, but persuasive - clear at the sentence level, structured at the paragraph level, and evidenced through the sources you bring in.
wOpen.signpostIntro: This course moves through five techniques that build on each other, from sentence-level clarity to genre awareness.
wOpen.signpostOutro: Each lesson pairs a worked example with a quick check, so you can see the technique in action before applying it yourself.

wClose.courseSummary: You have completed Academic Writing: Intermediate Stage - five techniques for writing with argument, structure, and sources.
wClose.practiceConnection: These techniques apply directly to your next piece of assessed writing: run your draft through the four pillars, check your paragraphs open with a claim, and make sure your own voice frames any sources you cite.
wClose.whereThisGoesNext: The Advanced stage builds on this by turning to how writing conventions differ across disciplines - chemistry, education, history - and developing a sharper critical edge in your own writing.
